content:
A different kind of technosignature

Searching for radio signals assumes alien civilizations are broadcasting at the precise moment humanity is listening. Pinault’s team bypasses that timing problem by looking for physical evidence. Instead of signals, they want to find microscopic debris, fragments shed by spacecraft, industrial plants, or propulsion systems over millions of years. These particles can drift through interstellar space for millions of years before settling onto solid ground.

The idea builds on work by Ukrainian astronomer Oleksiy Arkhipov. In the 1990s, Arkhipov proposed that spacefaring cultures would naturally leave a physical footprint behind. He reasoned that over eons, stray spacecraft fragments and industrial exhaust would drift across star systems. Arkhipov reasoned that this debris would eventually settle on stable bodies like the Moon. Planetary scientist Lewis Pinault and his co-authors — Brian Lacki, Ian Crawford, and Andrew Siemion — took that concept and developed it into a practical, testable search protocol.

Why the moon holds onto everything

Earth is a poor record keeper. Rain, wind, and volcanic eruptions continuously recycle the planet’s crust. Tectonic subduction then swallows the surface, erasing almost all physical evidence of the planet’s past within a few hundred million years. The Moon possesses none of these destructive mechanisms. Lacking an atmosphere, weather, or internal geological engine, its surface remains virtually static. Neil Armstrong’s bootprint from the 1969 Apollo 11 landing remains intact today, threatened only by rare micrometeorite. Over eons, cosmic impacts slowly churn the top layer of lunar soil in a process known as impact gardening. Beneath that surface layer, the regolith acts as a cold storage vault. It has preserved interstellar material accumulated continuously over nearly 4.5 billion years.

How the search would work

The research team proposes collecting one cubic meter of lunar soil, which weighs about 1.5 metric tons. Rather than sorting through the dust manually, scientists would deploy high-throughput electron microscopy, X-ray micro-tomography, and spectroscopy. Machine-learning algorithms would then scan the data to flag non-natural geometries or anomalous elemental alloys. The paper makes no claim that alien technosignatures are present in current Apollo or Luna samples. It establishes a mathematical framework: if researchers analyze a full cubic meter of regolith and find zero non-terrestrial synthetic particles, that negative result establishes the first empirical upper limit on the density of artificial debris scattered across our galactic neighborhood. Upcoming sample-return missions planned under NASA’s Artemis program and China’s Chang’e program could make a sample harvest of this scale technically feasible for the first time.

Building on autonomous probe theory

The regolith proposal connects directly to historical debates over how civilizations expand through the cosmos. In 1960, physicist Ronald Bracewell argued that interstellar communication via radio was inefficient at that scale. He suggested advanced cultures would instead dispatch autonomous, long-lived probes to monitor neighboring star systems. Decades later, researchers expanded that idea into self-replicating von Neumann probes—machines designed to harvest raw materials from asteroids and moons to construct copies of themselves. If such autonomous networks ever navigated the Milky Way, their construction, operation, or eventual degradation would leave behind a micro-particle footprint.

As SETI Institute CEO Bill Diamond pointed out, Pinault’s framework moves the debate out of theory and onto the ground, giving researchers a physical target to test.

Existing technology, pending samples

Every analytical instrument required for the project already exists and operates daily in materials science and meteorology laboratories worldwide. Advanced mass spectrometers can easily isolate terrestrial contaminants from cosmic material, and optical algorithms routinely sort billions of particles in industrial settings. The biggest obstacle is access to the raw material. Scientists have never brought a cubic meter of lunar soil back to Earth, let alone processed one under strict cleanroom conditions to prevent contamination. Researchers emphasize that while a negative finding simply refines theoretical limits on galactic civilizations, any positive candidate would undergo years of multi-laboratory verification before standing as definitive evidence of non-terrestrial origin.

Sources: Lewis J. Pinault et al., “Micron-Scale Technosignatures: How a Cubic Metre of Lunar Regolith May Begin to Constrain the Number of Past Technological Civilisations in the Galaxy,” International Journal of Astrobiology, in press; arXiv:2606.24028; SETI Institute press statement.
